title: Lanterns
hookLine: Vesak lanterns in Sri Lanka, lotus lanterns in Korea: light for the many

lines: COLOMBO: A LANTERN AT EVERY GATE.
SEOUL: A RIVER OF LOTUS LIGHTS.
LIGHT WHERE OTHERS CAN SEE IT.
cards: Two cities on the Buddha's day.
In Colombo at dusk, every house seems to have hung something in the window or over the gate: paper lanterns in stars and octagons, bamboo frames covered in colored tissue, swaying in the warm air.
In Seoul, a river of light pours down one of the city's big avenues: crowds carrying lanterns shaped like lotus flowers, dragons, elephants, the baby Buddha.
Two countries, two different Buddhist traditions, the same instinct: make light, and put it where others can see it.

teach.h: SRI LANKA: THE KUDU AND THE THORANA.
teach.b: In Sri Lanka, the Vesak lantern is called a kudu. Families often make their own from thin bamboo sticks and colored paper, and there are competitions for the most beautiful.
Streets are also lined with huge lit gateways, called thoranas or pandals, painted with scenes from the Jataka stories you met in the stories camp, and blazing with colored bulbs.

In Korea, the lantern festival is called Yeondeunghoe, the gathering for lighting lanterns. Its records reach back to the old Korean kingdoms, and in 2020 UNESCO recognized it as part of the world's living heritage.
Temples hang rows of lotus lanterns across their courtyards, many with small paper tags carrying the names and wishes of the families who offered them. Why lanterns?

You know part of the answer: two days ago, the lamp people light on Vesak; last week, light as a picture of wisdom; and before that, Nanda's lamp. But a lantern adds something a candle on a shrine doesn't.
It's hung outside, over the gate, carried through the streets.
The light is for whoever walks by: neighbors, strangers, people of every faith and none. Nobody asks who deserves to see it.
That echoes a line in the old texts: the Buddha, they say, taught out of compassion for the world, for the good of the many. A lantern in the window is that idea made of paper and bamboo.

how: On the Buddha's day, Sri Lankan families hang handmade Vesak lanterns and cities build illuminated gateways, while in Korea temples hang lotus lanterns and Seoul holds the Yeondeunghoe lantern parade.

games.why: lanterns go where passersby can see them: over gates, in windows, along streets. the light is for the many.

practice: Picture a paper lantern, any shape you like, a lotus, a star, a simple box, glowing outside your front door or in your window.
Let whoever passes tonight walk through its light: a neighbor, a delivery driver, a child on the way home. Wish each one well: may you be safe, may you be at ease.

wordCard.voice: Lanterns. Vesak lanterns in Sri Lanka, lotus lanterns in Korea: light hung where everyone passing can see it.

orig.note: Korean: 'lantern-lighting gathering', the lotus lantern festival for the Buddha's birthday.

carryVoice: Your line: light for the many. A lantern in the window doesn't ask who's walking by. One hundred forty-seven days now.

sources.ref: Vinaya, Mahavagga I.11, teaching 'for the good of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world'
